results.name: shared_digit_set_nonmatching_same_parity
results.description: On 3-4 example sets whose examples all share a last digit, yes rate for non-example targets with a different last digit but the same parity as the examples; observed below null means the model leaks too much generalization to same-parity numbers (via odd/even, contains-digit, prime rules) when an ends-in-digit rule fits.
results.code:
# name: shared_digit_set_nonmatching_same_parity
# description: On 3-4 example sets whose examples all share a last digit, yes rate for non-example targets with a different last digit but the same parity as the examples; observed below null means the model leaks too much generalization to same-parity numbers (via odd/even, contains-digit, prime rules) when an ends-in-digit rule fits.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    U = E % 10; tu = t % 10
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0
    same_u = np.nanmax(U, axis=1) == np.nanmin(U, axis=1)
    m = (n >= 3) & same_u & ~is_ex & (tu != U[:, 0]) & (t % 2 == E[:, 0] % 2)
    return rate(m)

results.name: ruleless_three_plus_in_range_rate
results.description: On 3-4 example sets that no rule (odd/even, multiples 3-12, powers 2-10, squares, cubes, primes, ends-in/contains digit) fits fully, yes rate for in-range non-example targets; observed above null means the model under-generalizes within the examples' range when no rule explains the examples.
results.code:
# name: ruleless_three_plus_in_range_rate
# description: On 3-4 example sets that no rule (odd/even, multiples 3-12, powers 2-10, squares, cubes, primes, ends-in/contains digit) fits fully, yes rate for in-range non-example targets; observed above null means the model under-generalizes within the examples' range when no rule explains the examples.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    U = E % 10; tu = t % 10
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0
    def fits(member):
        ok = np.ones(len(t), dtype=bool)
        for j in range(4):
            v = E[:, j]
            ok &= np.isnan(v) | member(np.nan_to_num(v).astype(int))
        return ok
    any_fit = fits(lambda v: v % 2 == 1) | fits(lambda v: v % 2 == 0)
    for mm in range(3, 13):
        any_fit |= fits(lambda v, mm=mm: v % mm == 0)
    sets = [{i * i for i in range(1, 11)}, {1, 8, 27, 64},
            {p for p in range(2, 101) if all(p % q for q in range(2, int(p ** 0.5) + 1))}]
    for b in range(2, 11):
        sets.append({b ** k for k in range(1, 8) if b ** k <= 100})
    for s in sets:
        arr = np.zeros(101, dtype=bool); arr[list(s)] = True
        any_fit |= fits(lambda v, arr=arr: arr[np.clip(v, 0, 100)])
    for d in range(10):
        any_fit |= fits(lambda v, d=d: v % 10 == d)
        any_fit |= fits(lambda v, d=d: (v % 10 == d) | ((v // 10) % 10 == d) | ((d == 0) & (v == 100)) | ((d == 1) & (v == 100)))
    m = (n >= 3) & ~any_fit & ~is_ex & (t >= lo) & (t <= hi)
    return rate(m)

results.name: two_example_shared_digit_match_minus_nonmatch
results.description: On two-example sets whose examples share a last digit, yes rate for non-example targets with that last digit minus yes rate for same-parity targets with another last digit; observed above null means people pick up the ends-in-digit rule from a pair more sharply than the model predicts, below null means less sharply.
results.code:
# name: two_example_shared_digit_match_minus_nonmatch
# description: On two-example sets whose examples share a last digit, yes rate for non-example targets with that last digit minus yes rate for same-parity targets with another last digit; observed above null means people pick up the ends-in-digit rule from a pair more sharply than the model predicts, below null means less sharply.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    U = E % 10; tu = t % 10
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0
    same_u = np.nanmax(U, axis=1) == np.nanmin(U, axis=1)
    base = (n == 2) & same_u & ~is_ex
    return rate(base & (tu == U[:, 0])) - rate(base & (tu != U[:, 0]) & (t % 2 == E[:, 0] % 2))

results.name: narrow_minus_wide_span_in_range
results.description: On 2+ example sets, yes rate for in-range non-example targets when the examples span at most 30 minus when they span more than 60; observed below null means the model over-endorses the interior of narrow example ranges (tight intervals) or under-endorses the interior of wide ones relative to people.
results.code:
# name: narrow_minus_wide_span_in_range
# description: On 2+ example sets, yes rate for in-range non-example targets when the examples span at most 30 minus when they span more than 60; observed below null means the model over-endorses the interior of narrow example ranges (tight intervals) or under-endorses the interior of wide ones relative to people.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    U = E % 10; tu = t % 10
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0
    span = hi - lo
    base = (n >= 2) & ~is_ex & (t >= lo) & (t <= hi)
    return rate(base & (span <= 30)) - rate(base & (span > 60))

results.name: single_example_near_minus_far
results.description: On one-example sets, yes rate for non-example targets within 10 of the example minus yes rate for targets more than 40 away; observed below null means people show less magnitude-proximity generalization from a single example than the model's interval concepts predict (observed is roughly flat/negative).
results.code:
# name: single_example_near_minus_far
# description: On one-example sets, yes rate for non-example targets within 10 of the example minus yes rate for targets more than 40 away; observed below null means people show less magnitude-proximity generalization from a single example than the model's interval concepts predict (observed is roughly flat/negative).
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    U = E % 10; tu = t % 10
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0
    d = np.abs(t - E[:, 0])
    base = (n == 1) & ~is_ex
    return rate(base & (d <= 10)) - rate(base & (d > 40))

results.name: single_example_shared_digit_minus_none
results.description: On one-example sets, yes rate for non-example targets sharing the example's units or tens digit minus yes rate for targets sharing neither digit; observed above null means the model's single-example discount of digit rules is too strong (people generalize by shared digits from one example more than predicted), below null means too weak.
results.code:
# name: single_example_shared_digit_minus_none
# description: On one-example sets, yes rate for non-example targets sharing the example's units or tens digit minus yes rate for targets sharing neither digit; observed above null means the model's single-example discount of digit rules is too strong (people generalize by shared digits from one example more than predicted), below null means too weak.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    U = E % 10; tu = t % 10
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0
    tt = t // 10; T0 = E[:, 0] // 10
    share = (tu == U[:, 0]) | ((tt == T0) & (t < 100) & (E[:, 0] < 100))
    base = (n == 1) & ~is_ex
    return rate(base & share) - rate(base & ~share)

results.name: prime_set_prime_minus_odd_nonprime
results.description: On 2+ example sets whose examples are all prime, yes rate for prime non-example targets minus yes rate for odd non-prime targets; observed below null means the model credits the prime rule more sharply than people, who barely separate primes from other odd numbers.
results.code:
# name: prime_set_prime_minus_odd_nonprime
# description: On 2+ example sets whose examples are all prime, yes rate for prime non-example targets minus yes rate for odd non-prime targets; observed below null means the model credits the prime rule more sharply than people, who barely separate primes from other odd numbers.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    U = E % 10; tu = t % 10
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0
    P = np.array([k > 1 and all(k % q for q in range(2, int(k ** 0.5) + 1)) for k in range(101)])
    Ei = np.clip(np.nan_to_num(E).astype(int), 0, 100)
    allp = np.all(np.isnan(E) | P[Ei], axis=1)
    ti = t.astype(int)
    base = (n >= 2) & allp & ~is_ex
    return rate(base & P[ti]) - rate(base & ~P[ti] & (ti % 2 == 1))

results.name: two_example_parity_gap_in_range
results.description: On two-example sets with same-parity examples but different last digits, yes rate for in-range non-example targets of the examples' parity minus the rate for opposite-parity in-range targets; observed above null means the model under-uses parity from a pair (people restrict to the shared parity more), below null means it over-uses it.
results.code:
# name: two_example_parity_gap_in_range
# description: On two-example sets with same-parity examples but different last digits, yes rate for in-range non-example targets of the examples' parity minus the rate for opposite-parity in-range targets; observed above null means the model under-uses parity from a pair (people restrict to the shared parity more), below null means it over-uses it.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    U = E % 10; tu = t % 10
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0
    same_u = np.nanmax(U, axis=1) == np.nanmin(U, axis=1)
    P = E % 2
    same_p = np.nanmax(P, axis=1) == np.nanmin(P, axis=1)
    base = (n == 2) & same_p & ~same_u & ~is_ex & (t >= lo) & (t <= hi)
    return rate(base & (t % 2 == E[:, 0] % 2)) - rate(base & (t % 2 != E[:, 0] % 2))
